notes: This is the LIKE-FOR-LIKE comparison: quality-matched to a shop-machined neck, and the only purchase reference the make case should be judged against.
Landed cost is unknown. Domestic or import status is unstated, so neither freight nor duty is assumed.
NOT A LIKE-FOR-LIKE SUBSTITUTE and must not be compared as one.
Owner assessment: the workmanship may not pass inspection at all, in which case it is not an option at any price.
The fingerboard is probably composite, against AAA ebony at 29.00 on the in-house spec it was being compared with.

EVERY LANDED-COST FIELD IS UNKNOWN. Freight, duty under HTS 9209 plus any Section 301 line which must be verified current, incoming inspection, corrective fretwork and reject rate all sit between 45.00 and a usable neck.
A modelled hidden-cost structure suggests these roughly double the catalog figure, but nothing in it is measured, which is why no value is recorded here.

Heel-to-pocket fit is the specific risk for a CNC shop: the neck pocket is repeatable to hundredths of a millimetre and an imported heel is not. That mismatch costs labour on every instrument, not once.

threshold_findings.sign_convention: difference_versus_threshold = threshold_price - maximum_compatible_delivered_purchase_price. POSITIVE means buying at that price costs more than building, i.e. make is lower cost. Retained shop work sits on the BUY side, which is why the ceiling is below the make cost.

matrices.description: Fretboard stock price against fretwork minutes. The pair of levers the accepted sprint identified, retained here because both remain valid.
Fretwork minutes against saleable yield. Fretwork is the largest labour operation and yield is wholly unmeasured, so this is the pair with the most unknown between them.

Machine runtime per neck against saleable yield. Added by GAP-CLOSURE-1: runtime previously had no yield axis and never rose above the unverified 52-minute baseline, so the model could not show what a WORSE runtime does to a batch that also loses necks.

findings.metric: cost per saleable neck, quantity 1 to 40
findings.interpretation: Only one operation in the neck carries setup, so batching is worth 9.34 per neck and no more. The router capacity that prompted this sprint is not the constraint.

findings.metric: one-piece versus scarf-jointed, M4 at quantity 20
findings.interpretation: The headstock-angle decision moves more money than every batching effect combined, and it is a design choice rather than a process one.

findings.metric: fretwork minutes required to beat the boutique price
findings.interpretation: Fretwork is the largest single operation at 78 minutes, and a fret press with batch jigs is the only credible way to reduce it. But it is no longer sufficient: at a COMPLETE neck, taking fretwork to zero still leaves in-house above the boutique price.

findings.metric: cost per saleable at a free fretboard, fretwork unchanged
findings.interpretation: BOTH LEVERS AT THEIR LIMIT STILL MISS. A free fretboard AND zero fretwork together leave in-house above the boutique price at a complete neck. An earlier table suggested otherwise; it costed an UNFINISHED neck against a finished purchased one, before fretboard installation and neck finishing existed in the model. Those two operations and a 90% yield close the gap off.

The 45.00 import is not a like-for-like substitute: probable composite fingerboard against AAA ebony, and the owner judges the workmanship may not pass inspection at all. Every landed-cost field is unknown. It is recorded as a reference, not as a comparison.

findings.metric: labour minutes affordable against a back-calculated manufacturing cost
findings.interpretation: Working backwards from an observed shelf price puts a manufacturer's cost between 51.30 and 96.19. To meet the typical-channel figure this shop must build a complete neck in about 23 labour minutes against 191 today, or pay about 3.46 an hour against 28.75. Two of the four routes are unreachable on materials and machine time ALONE, before any labour. The gap is labour RATE times CONTENT, and the shop can only move content - which needs an eightfold reduction, not a process tweak.

findings.metric: threshold comparisons that are commercially actionable
findings.interpretation: B1-B4 are now defined and every threshold from 90 to 140 is judged like-for-like against its make state. NOT ONE COMPARISON IS ACTIONABLE. The instrument is headless with a locking clamp nut at 628.65 mm, and no supplier of such a neck has been identified at any completion state. The economics are computed anyway, because a threshold the shop cannot act on today is still the number it would need if a source appeared.

findings.metric: cost per saleable neck across the widened runtime grid
findings.interpretation: The accepted runtime sweep only descended from the unverified 52-minute baseline, so it could only ever show the number proving favourable. Extended above it, the grid shows the spread across the full domain. Runtime remains the largest single unmeasured lever and it now cuts both ways.

findings.metric: reachable threshold combinations against the boutique price
findings.interpretation: In-house does NOT beat a quality-matched purchased neck at a complete state, by any combination of the levers this sprint identified. That conclusion rests on two draft operations that have never been measured, so the measurement that would overturn it is fretboard installation and neck finishing time, not batching.
